props.title: They Were Eleven

sections.content: **They Were Eleven** (1986) stands as a masterpiece of psychological sci-fi anime, building tension through a premise that echoes later works like **Moon** (2009) and **Cube** (1997). The story of 10 students who discover an 11th member during their final exam aboard a derelict spaceship creates immediate paranoia and suspicion. Director Satō Dezaki brings the same psychological complexity he showed in **The Rose of Versailles** (1979), crafting a pressure-cooker environment where identity and trust become increasingly unstable.

sections.content: The film's examination of gender identity through character Frol was groundbreaking for 1986, predating mainstream handling of such themes by decades. This complexity rivals later works like **Ghost in the Shell** (1995) and **Metropolis** (2001) in its exploration of identity and humanity. The confined setting creates claustrophobic tension similar to **Alien** (1979), while the mystery element draws parallels to **The Thing** (1982).

The film's visual style showcases the height of hand-drawn anime craftsmanship, with detailed spaceship designs and character animation that influenced later works like **Cowboy Bebop: The Movie** (2001) and **Planetes** (2003). The attention to scientific detail and space physics recalls **2001: A Space Odyssey** (1968), while maintaining the human drama at its core. SUBHEAD: Educational Sci-Fi Evolution

sections.content: **They Were Eleven** (1986) represents a crucial evolution in educational sci-fi, following the tradition of works like **Royal Space Force: The Wings of Honnêamise** (1987) while predating later examples like **Planetes** (2003). The film's integration of complex scientific concepts with character drama created a template for intelligent sci-fi anime that influenced works like **Steins;Gate** (2011) and **Knights of Sidonia** (2014).
